text: Aleksei Morozov / Age: 37
Rank/Position: Junior Sergeant, deputy squad leader
Civilian Occupation: Tractor driver (kolkhoz)
Origin: Kursk region, RSFSR
Aleksei Morozov was kept alive by hatred.
Not hatred for the Hungarians across the river,
or the occasional German you could spot among them.
Those men were just obstacles, things standing between him and whatever counted as home now.
What pumped blood through his veins, day after day, moment after moment,
was contempt for his uncle. For how he ruined his family.
Aleksei's father was a simple, hard-working man,
a man who spent his whole life farming and tending animals.
He didn't understand big politics, and he didn't want to.
He believed that anything he needed, he could produce with his own hands.
For a long time, it looked like the world would prove him right,
because his patience and his discipline built a respectable fortune,
which, by some small miracle, even survived the chaos of the civil war years,
despite the state taking whatever it could from the countryside.
But since his father never watched the world, only his own farm,
the burden fell onto Aleksei and his mother, Anna,
to warn him that collectivization was inevitable,
and that they should sell the equipment, the threshing machine and the livestock
while they still could,
so that with the money they could get out of the country as soon as possible.
Aleksei's father may have seen the logic in his family's words,
but the thought of leaving his country,
and of the dangers that came with it, must have terrified him.
That's probably why he listened to his younger brother, Pyotr, who insisted
that better days would come, that there was no need to panic,
only to hide what they could, so that later,
when those better days arrived, there would be something left to reach for.
Aleksei's father trusted his brother. Why wouldn't he?
He didn't even know that Pyotr had already joined the Komsomol,
the Soviet communist youth organization,
and was nursing far-reaching political ambitions.
And nothing built a ladder for those ambitions faster
than discovering — and smoking out — a kulak.
So Pyotr wrote a florid speech that played on the community's emotions,
and then delivered it in a trembling voice, fighting back tears,
at the organization's first quarterly meeting of 1930,
which Aleksei of course did not attend,
but some of his acquaintances, later close friends, did,
and from their accounts he pictured the outrageous scene so many times
that he could see the smallest twitch in his uncle's face,
as if he had been standing right there
when the man betrayed his own brother — Aleksei's father.
The brigade, armed to the teeth, showed up at Aleksei's home the very next morning,
and they didn't stop until they had turned the place upside down
and found everything on the list Pyotr had given them.
What made it worse was that the family hadn't just sat on their wealth,
they had hidden it. The whole family was deported,
party functionaries moved into their home,
and Pyotr was made brigade leader.
From that day on, a large letter “K” stood out in Aleksei's papers,
branding not only him but the life of the son born three years later,
since the terrible stigma sat there in the boy's class register too.
Aleksei's father couldn't carry the weight of the betrayal.
He hanged himself.
His mother didn't last much longer; grief and shame finished what the state had started.
Aleksei became a tractor driver and for years he planned revenge against his uncle,
putting it off again and again for the sake of his family…
until the war came and he had to give it up entirely.
Soldiering, and the horrors he lived through, took so much from him
that he no longer let the possible consequences of a blood feud bother him.
So now, on this icy no-man's-land, it is the promise of future retribution that moves his limbs.
The faith that a day will come when he can take the rifle he holds right now,
press the barrel into the mouth of his uncle — who has since made an enviable political career —
and squeeze the trigger.
